question: Is the air better in the north or the west of Singapore right now?
name: Claude
answer:
The air is better in the **north** right now, though both regions are in the unhealthy range because of ongoing haze.

**Latest readings (NEA, 7am on 17 Oct):**

| Region | 24-hr PSI | 1-hr PM2.5 (µg/m³) |
|---|---|---|
| North | 144 (Unhealthy) | 83 (Elevated) |
| West | 181 (Unhealthy) | 97 (Elevated) |

At 7am, the 24-hour PSI was in the "unhealthy" range in all regions: central (191), north (144), south (161), east (175), west (181). PM2.5 shows what the air is like at the moment, and it was also lower in the north: north (83), south (75), east (119), west (97).

**Background:**
- The north has been the least affected region throughout this haze episode. On 16 Oct, the west hit the "very unhealthy" level (204 in the west at 6pm), while the north stayed lower (6pm readings of 162 in the north).
- The west recorded the worst moment of the season: the highest PM2.5 reading this haze season was recorded at 3pm on Oct 14 in the western part of the island at 288.
- Neither region has clean air. If you need clean air, the south currently has the lowest PM2.5 of all regions.

**Health advice:** With PSI in the unhealthy range, NEA advises people to cut down on long or strenuous outdoor activity. Children, older people, pregnant women and anyone with heart or lung conditions should take extra care.

These numbers change every hour. For the latest readings, check haze.gov.sg or the NEA / myENV app.

Singapore has now endured nearly two weeks of unhealthy air quality in at least part of the island. The last time all five regions recorded moderate air quality simultaneously was at midnight on Oct 5, when 24-hour PSI readings ranged from 77 to 100.

# Singapore haze pushes air quality to very unhealthy levels in three regions
**Air quality worsened across Singapore overnight, with the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) readings reaching the very unhealthy range in three regions on Friday (Oct 16).**

Central Singapore was the first to cross into the very unhealthy band at midnight, and its 24-hour PSI climbed to 229 at 3pm – the highest reading recorded this year, according to Channel NewsAsia.

The east and west entered the band at 10am, with readings of 202 and 201 respectively. At 6pm, the PSI stood at 204 in the west, 203 in the east, and 227 in the central region.



Air quality remained unhealthy in the other two regions, with 6pm readings of 162 in the north and 182 in the south.

Hourly PM2.5 readings were high in central and southern Singapore at 191 and 163, respectively. The other regions recorded elevated readings of between 134 and 147.

SINGAPORE, March 26 — Singapore woke up to hazy skies this morning, with air quality registering in the moderate range, according to the National Environment Agency (NEA).

The Straits Times (ST) reported that at 9am, the country’s Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) readings ranged from 61 to 75, with the highest levels recorded in the central region.

This comes after a warning from the Asean Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) on March 17 about a heightened risk of severe transboundary haze due to prolonged dry weather and increased hot spot activity across the region, ST added.

Satellite data showed extensive fire activity in Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam, with 2,177 and 1,941 hot spots detected on March 15 and 16, respectively.

According to ST, Singapore remains in its north-east monsoon season, with prevailing winds from the north-west and north-east.



These conditions make it possible for smoke plumes from the northern parts of South-east Asia to be carried towards the city-state.

Despite the moderate PSI readings, one-hour PM2.5 levels remained within the normal range. PM2.5, a fine particulate matter, is the primary pollutant during transboundary haze episodes.

A PSI reading between 51 and 100 is considered moderate, while levels above 100 indicate unhealthy air quality.

When PSI reaches the unhealthy range (101-200), authorities advise reducing prolonged outdoor activities, especially for vulnerable groups such as the elderly, pregnant women
